To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

visuospatially trained participants were more likely than symbolically trained participants to form visuospatial mental representations of math problems, which in turn led to more active imagery/sematic areas in the first two stages of solving.

learners trained on novel math problems with a symbolic definition versus a visuospatial definition, when later solving problems in a scanner, exhibited distinct activations across four stages identified via an HSMM‐based process (Anderson and Fitcham, 2015a).

Learners solved identical problems (via symbolic or visuospratial mental strategies), and that HSMM‐MVPCA applied to fMRI revealed 4 distinct stages during solving (encode, plan, compute and respond), in which visuospatially trained learners had more active areas in the semantic/imagery network (during encoding), and in the precuneus (during computation).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question how does processing differ during problem solving, when mathematical operations are associated with meaningful visuospatial representations versus when the operations are defined strictly symbolically?

the question of whether there are any brain regions that are more active when solving math problems in which the operands are represented in terms of visuospatial dimensions, rather than purely symbolically, even when the visuospatial representations are not displayed.
the question of how learners process mathematical operations, when they can be associated with meaningful referents versus being strictly symbolic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the visuospatially trained group had more activation in areas related to mental imagery and semantic processing during encoding and computation, and the symbolically trained group had more frontal and temporal activation during planning.

visuospatially-trained learners were more active in brain regions associated with semantic processing and mental imagery, especially in the encoding and computation stages, while symbolically-trained learners showed greater activity in frontal and parietal brain regions during the planning stage.
the visuospatial group has more active semantic areas in the first 2 stages of solving, and more active imagery areas in the third stage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visuospatial group used mental visuospatial images to solve the problems. The symbolic group used only the symbols to solve the problem.
the visuospatially trained learners were more active in areas involved in semantic processing and/or imagery during the encoding stage, and in areas involved in computation during the compute stage.
visuospatial representations of the problem can be used to help solve the problems, even when no visuospatial cues are present during the actual solving process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mental visuospatial imagery may not only inform initial problem encoding but may also scaffold on‐going symbolic computation.
the brain regions involved in solving a math operation can be different depending on whether the operation has visuospatial meanings or not.
mental visuospatial representation is not only important in the initial interpretation of a problem, but may also scaffold on‐going symbolic computations.
